result.verdict:
One real regression, in the three.js renderer only: the gear's motion vectors (velocity) are wrong while it retracts. The rest of the shader and uniform code checks out.

What I verified with headless Chromium on three r186, building the realMaterial positionNode exactly as committed:
- **Generated shader code.** The GLSL is correct for the main, shadow and prepass vertex stages. The WGSL compiled with no errors on the WebGPU backend (SwiftShader).
- **Shadow pass.** It uses the same positionNode (three.debug.js:64212-64215 and 64310), so shadows follow the deformation. The old renderer's shadow program uses the same ACR_VS and gets each item's uniforms (js/renderer.js:49, :186).
- **Normals.** `normalLocal = nodeVar1` is written before `v_normalViewGeometry` is computed. Read-back normals match the expected rotation exactly: starboard main leg at progress 0.5 gives rgb (128,39,219), port gives (128,216,219), expected (128,39,219) and (128,216,219).
- **Vertex order in the rotation.** TSL cached dx, dy and dz into temporaries before `p.x` / `p.y` are reassigned.
- **Collapse test.** It recomputes `leg` inline, so it never reads the uninitialised `nodeVar4` when uGearT is 0.
- **Old renderer GLSL.** ACR_VS compiles under WebGL2 with the includes stubbed.

Regression questions:
- **Models without their own gear.** Only b738, b772 and b77w have hasGear. On every other model `extra.x` stays an integer, so leg = 0. With uGearT = 0 the collapse condition is the same as the old `select`.
- **Zone decoding elsewhere.** Every decode rounds with +0.5: ACR_VS:21, ACR_FS:66 and js/three/aircraft.js:46. No JS or tool code reads `extra` from the decoded model.
- **Fractional values.** Codes go up to 0.4, so the zone never flips. `int(3.4 + 0.5)` is 3 and the leg comes out as 4.
- **NaN.** `top()` always counts at least the top vertex itself, and every cluster has at least one vertex, so there is no divide by zero.
- **Uniforms.** realUniforms always sets uGearT and uGearRig, using 0 and [0,0,0,0] when there is no rig.

Load cost: gearRig takes 10-60 ms per model decode on this machine (b738 32-59 ms, b77w 17-23 ms, b772 10-16 ms). The flood-fill and per-cluster statistics phase takes 17-30 ms of that. It runs once per model decode. The largest cell holds 1,616 vertices, well below the argument limits for the spread calls. This is acceptable, so I have not listed it as a finding.

Test scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Calc/3fd08d73-28ea-592f-8f33-69ede4de867b/scratchpad/gearrev/ and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Calc/3fd08d73-28ea-592f-8f33-69ede4de867b/scratchpad/www/tgear.html.

findings.problem: The new positionNode moves gear vertices (positionLocal) but leaves three's positionPrevious at the original geometry position. Velocity is computed as current deformed position minus previous undeformed position, so every gear and door pixel reports a motion vector equal to its whole rotation offset, not the change since the last frame. On every shipped TRAA tier (ultra, high, medium prepass; low MRT), TRAA then reprojects history from the wrong place and adds a large motion factor. Expect lost anti-aliasing, jitter shimmer and ghosting on the legs during retraction, which is exactly what the d_gearup film shot shows. The low tier also takes its AO from the previous frame at screenUV - velocity (engine.js:304), so gear pixels get AO from the wrong spot. Before this commit the gear only collapsed to a point and drew no pixels, so this is new. The old renderer is fine: ACR_VS builds both wp and pwp from the deformed p.
findings.evidence: three.debug.js:38857 `positionPrevious = positionGeometry.toVarying("positionPrevious")` and :51409 `clipPositionPrevious = ...mul(positionPrevious)`, while the current clip position uses positionLocal (:51408). Captured GLSL of a velocity MRT pass: `positionLocal = nodeVar0;` ... `positionPrevious = position;`. Measured in headless Chromium with a static camera and object, gearT held at 0.5 across both frames, nose code 3.1: the velocity texel at the centre is (-0.68, 0.27); it should be (0, 0). A non-gear vertex (code 0) or gearT = 0 gives (0, 0). TRAA uses this velocity for historyUV and motionFactor (three.debug.js:83408-83426). MRTs with velocity: engine.js:265, 270, 291.
findings.fix: Inside the positionNode Fn, take the builder and also deform the previous position when velocity is needed: `m.positionNode = Fn((builder) => { ...; TSL.normalLocal.assign(n); if (builder.needsPreviousData()) TSL.positionPrevious.assign(p); return p; })();`. This is the same pattern three's Line2NodeMaterial uses (three.debug.js:42190-42191). I ran it headless: the spurious velocity becomes (0, 0) and the rotated normals are unchanged. It matches the old renderer, where only body motion counts. For exact gear motion vectors, add a per-object `gearTPrev` uniform (last frame's eased progress) and apply the same rotation with it to positionPrevious.

result.verdict:
The rotation signs are correct, and the GLSL and TSL formulas match. The nose leg swings toward +x, both mains swing toward z=0, and normals use the same rotation (1.4923 = 0.95*pi/2, 1.5394 = 0.98*pi/2). Every zone-3 vertex gets the correct side code (code 2 has z<0, code 3 has z>0). node tools/models/test_gear_rig.mjs passes.

The pivots and fold angles that gearRig takes from the meshes are wrong, and this shows on screen. I checked by rotating the actual vertices, after applyStretch for each type, with the shader formulas and ray-casting them against the zone 0/5 skin:
(1) On every 777 variant the nose tyres are still up to 0.78 m below the forward belly at full retraction.
(2) The 737 nose pivot comes from the zone-3 nose wheel-well box, not from the strut, and it changes between variants. On the B37M the folded nose tyres hang up to 0.89 m below the radome.
(3) The main-leg pivot |z| averages the strut top with the side-brace top, so it sits 0.45 m (737) or 0.98 m (777) inboard of the strut. The treads end on the centreline: they touch on the 737 and overlap by 5.3 cm on the 777. Braces swing up through the wing, up to 1.64 m above it on the 777. The outer tyres first drop 0.17 m (737) or 0.35 m (777).
(4) The 777's closed inboard belly doors stay put while the trucks cut through them.
(5) The test checks the unstretched geometry, not what ships, and checks no kinematic outcome.

findings.problem: On every 777 variant (B772, B773, B77W, B77L, B779) the nose leg never stows. The 85.5 deg fold (0.95*90) leaves the leg 4.5 deg below horizontal, but the forward belly rises about 9.6 deg. At full retraction the nose tyres hang below the fuselage. They then vanish at gear<=0.001, and on extension they pop in already hanging below.
findings.evidence: b77w (stretched) nose pivot is (-5.989, -2.163), at the strut top. Nose tyre vertices (lowest 1.1 m of leg 1), uGearT=1: box x[-3.82,-2.80] y[-3.17,-2.14]; 76 % of the vertices are below the zone-0/5 skin bottom, by up to 0.78 m (b772: 71 %, 0.72 m). At uGearT=0.9: 100 % below, by up to 1.14 m. Belly (centreline ray): y -2.89 at x=-6, -2.38 at x=-3. Fold-angle sweep with the same pivot: 90 deg is 0.57 m below, 100 deg is 0.10 m below, 105 deg is fully inside (-0.14 m). js/three/aircraft.js:58 uses the same 0.95 factor.
findings.fix: Fit the nose fold angle per model instead of the procedural gear's 0.95*90 deg: about 105 deg for the 777 with this pivot. Better, solve it from the mesh so the folded tyre box sits above the belly ray-cast. Pass it in the rig, e.g. as a 5th value, and add a test that the folded nose gear is inside the skin.

findings.problem: The 737 nose pivot is defined by the zone-3 nose wheel-well box, not by the strut. The box is single triangles forming walls at x=-2.45 and x=-4.54, |z| up to 0.75, and a ceiling at y -0.63..-0.82. The box rule (+1 unit) joins it to the nose leg, so the fixed well rotates with the leg, and its ceiling becomes the 'strut top'. The cell clustering runs after applyStretch, so the result varies by variant. The 0.149 gearUp shift moves the 0.5-unit cell boundaries. For B736/B737/B738/B739/B38M/B39M/B3XM, 42 forward-wall vertices drop out as static code 4 and the pivot jumps by 0.69 m. The B37M keeps the forward pivot, and its folded nose tyres hang under the radome.
findings.evidence: Raw b738: the nose strut axis is at x approx -4.31 (median of every slice) and the strut tops out at y approx -1.68. The pivot is (-3.454, -0.625), the mean x of the 66 vertices at x in {-4.54, -3.26, -2.45} within 0.4 m of the well ceiling: 0.86 m forward of the strut and 1.06 m above its top. The shipped rigs are B738 (-4.147, -0.565, 42 vertices code 4) and B37M (-3.454, -0.510, all code 1). B37M at uGearT=1: nose tyres x[-1.25,-0.54] y[-1.94,-1.21], 100 % below the skin (skin bottom -1.12 at x=-0.75), by up to 0.89 m. The tyre bottom also first drops 0.13 m (uGearT 0.2-0.3). B738 at uGearT=1: tyres at x[-2.28,-1.56], 0.9 m ahead of the well's forward wall (x=-2.45). They stay hidden inside the skin, but they are not in the well.
findings.fix: Keep the well structure out of the leg: join only pieces that overlap the strut cluster's own box, not box+1 m, or mark the well box static (code 4) on every variant. Take the nose pivot from the ground-reaching strut cluster: its top at x approx -4.31, y approx -1.68 + gearUp. Run the clustering on the unstretched positions and carry the codes through the stretch, so every variant gets the same assignment.

findings.problem: top() takes the main pivot |z| as the mean of every vertex within 0.4 m of the highest one. That mixes the strut top with the upper end of the inboard side brace (the 777's brace end is a separate 60-vertex piece joined by the box rule). The pivot therefore sits 0.45 m (737) or 0.98 m (777) inboard of the trunnion. Every folded point ends up about e lower and about e further inboard (e(Rz - z) with a=88 deg). The treads converge on the centreline, inside the hull/keel walls. Rigidly rotated brace parts inboard of the pivot swing up through the wing. The outboard tyres first move down.
findings.evidence: 737 top vertices: 111 at z 1.86-1.99 (side strut, y -1.34..-1.09) and 126 at z 2.7-2.96, giving a mean of 2.417. The lower strut slices have median z 2.85-2.88. 777: 18 at z 3.27 and 24 at z 5.4-5.8, mean 4.611; strut median |z| is 5.59. At uGearT=1: 737 starboard zmin -0.0001 and port zmax +0.0002, so the treads touch at z=0, and 54 % of folded tyre vertices are inboard of the lower-hull wall (|z|=0.58 at y -2.1..-1.9). 777: +/-0.027 m, so the trucks interpenetrate by 5.3 cm, and 11 % of tyre vertices are inside the keel walls at |z| 0.28-0.30 (y -3.2..-2.0). Above the wing: the 777 brace piece (orig |z| 2.95-3.27) reaches y +0.41..+0.71 at |z| 3.76-4.57. That is 1.64 m above the wing upper surface (1.07 m at uGearT=0.5). In total 338 vertices are above the top skin, max 1.85 m (b772: 332, 1.90 m). 737: 530 side-strut vertices up to 0.61 m above the upper wing skin (y -1.08, normal +y, at x -20.24, z 2.1-2.3). Dip: the lowest main point drops 0.17 m (737) or 0.35 m (777) at uGearT 0.2-0.3. It only returns to the static level at 0.5; with an on-axis pivot the dip would be about 0.06 / 0.08 m.
findings.fix: Take the main pivot from the ground-reaching strut cluster only (737 |z| approx 2.87, y approx -1.2; 777 |z| approx 5.6). Leave side braces and actuators out of the rigid rotation: fold them as a two-link brace or hide them during the swing. Fit the angle and pivot so the folded truck lies in the well. For the 737 that means outboard of the hull wall (|z| > 0.6). For the 777 it means between the keel walls (0.3) and the door edge (3.08) and below the well ceiling (y approx -1.6..-1.9). Add left/right clearance and above-wing checks to the test.

findings.problem: The 777's code-0 zone-4 doors are closed belly panels, and they stay static and closed throughout the swing. The main trucks pass straight through them. Once uGearUp is set, the doors collapse with the gear and leave the wheel well open. The doors vanishing at gear-up predates this commit; the clipping during the swing is new.
findings.evidence: Code-0 door geometry (b77w): y -3.43 at |z| 0.3-2.5, curving up to y -1.94 at |z| 3.08, over x[-39.28,-34.58]. These are closed doors. Starboard truck vertices (lowest 1.4 m, 8946) against the door surface (ray-cast): uGearT 0.5: 7254 below; 0.6: 903 above / 7905 below; 0.7: 3312 / 5366; 0.8: 5415 / 3438; 0.9: 7038 / 1602; 1.0: 7992 above, 0 below. So the truck cuts through the closed panels from about uGearT 0.55 to 0.95. With gear up the belly is open from |z| 0.3 to 3.08 over 4.7 m (shader line 33 collapses code 0).
findings.fix: Give the code-0 doors their own animation. Rotate each about its outboard hinge (|z| approx 3.08, y approx -1.94): open them before the truck reaches |z| < 3.08, and close them once it is stowed. Keep them drawn (closed) with gear up instead of collapsing them.

findings.problem: The test runs gearRig on the raw quantized positions. The app runs it after applyStretch (js/live/models.js:73-74), so the rig and codes that ship are not the ones tested. The assertions only check pivot ranges, so none of the kinematic defects above would fail the test.
findings.evidence: Tested b738 rig: -3.454, -0.625, -1.171, 2.417, with no code-4 vertices. The app's B738 rig (stretchFor('b738', 'b738'): gearUp 0.149, noseExt) is -4.147, -0.565, -1.022, 2.417, and 42 nose vertices go from code 1 to code 4. B37M gives -3.454, -0.510. The only geometric assertion is R[0] < 0 && R[0] > -0.3 L && R[3] > 0.5.
findings.fix: Run the test for each type through stretchFor/applyStretch, as the app does. Rotate the leg vertices by the shader formulas at progress 0.5 and 1 and assert that: folded tyres are inside the skin or well; port and starboard keep a clearance; nothing rises above the wing upper surface; and the lowest point never drops below its static level by more than a few centimetres.

result.verdict:
Root cause found. The pit is not a culled or missing terrain chunk, a level-of-detail bug, or a reservoir carve. It is a real hole in the height field, about 100 m deep, made by the NAIP shoreline override in Terrain.height() (js/world/terrain.js:288-290). The shoreline data (data/sfo_shore.js) wrongly marks part of the US-101 freeway as Bay water. That spot is a strip about 30-45 m wide and 220 m long at world x -2599..-2499, z -2149..-1939, touching the west edge of the NAIP coverage at x = -2600. The NAIP image there shows the US-101 / I-380 interchange.

height() lowers every NAIP water cell to the Bay floor (about -2.6 m) without checking the procedural ground underneath, which is 88-103 m of hill at that spot. On the mesh's own 15 m grid (buildMeshes, 15 m spacing within ±4200 m), the strip's vertices sit at -3 m while their neighbours sit at 90-105 m, so the walls are vertical. The west wall is a straight line along the coverage edge. The world-wide water plane at y = 0 (js/live/world.js:59-66) shows at the bottom as the dark floor.

The pit is about 740 m from the aircraft at (-2200, -1400), bearing about 332°, which matches the frames. Nothing here involves commit 98823b9.

The data error has two causes in tools/imagery/shore_naip.py:
- **Water rule.** The freeway asphalt passes the water test. Its 10 m box-filtered NDWI is 0.27 and its NIR is 82, against the script's own claim that asphalt stays at NDWI <= 0.20 with NIR >= 114.
- **Fill step.** binary_fill_holes (line 74) only fills regions that do not touch the array border. Elsewhere along US-101, the freeway "water" is enclosed by land and gets filled back to land. This piece touches the west border, so it stays "Bay water".

I checked this with a copy of the pipeline that writes nothing to the repo. It leaves exactly one non-land component of 2083 pixels (8332 m²) that touches only the west edge. Padding the west edge as land before fill_holes removes that component and changes no other pixel.

Every other NAIP-water region in the coverage is real water (NDWI 0.50-0.72, NIR 20-50). Those regions sit on procedural ground no higher than 8.5 m, so they drop at most 12 m. I did not edit or commit anything. The scratch scripts and the NAIP crop are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Calc/3fd08d73-28ea-592f-8f33-69ede4de867b/scratchpad/pit/.

findings.problem: Inside the NAIP coverage, Terrain.height() lowers any cell that shoreAt() classes as water (m < 0.5) to the Bay floor, h = min(h, -2.6 - 0.8*fbm). It never checks that the procedural ground there is coastal lowland. One wrongly classified water strip in the hills therefore becomes a 100 m deep, vertical-walled shaft: the dark rectangular pit in the climb-out frames.
findings.evidence:
I loaded js/world/terrain.js in headless Chromium (real canvas) and sampled height() on the mesh grid that buildMeshes([0,0],15) uses (x, z = -4200 + 15k). In the strip at x -2595..-2505, z -2145..-1950, the vertices are at -3 m. Their neighbours are at 90-105 m, and the same points without the NAIP override are 88-103 m. The regional SDF at (-2554, -2051) is +1964 m (deep inland). shoreAt() is 0.00 in the strip and 1.00 around it. It is -1 for x < -2598.75 (line 217), so the west wall is a straight line between grid lines -2610 (101-102 m) and -2595 (-3 m). The water plane at y = 0 (js/live/world.js:61, 66) forms the dark floor.

A scan of the whole coverage at 10 m finds that all legitimate NAIP-water components have pre-override h <= 8.5 m and a drop of at most 11.8 m. This one component (8200 m², centre (-2554, -2051)) has pre-override h of 87.6-102.6 m and a drop of up to 105.6 m. San Andreas Lake's carve box ends at z >= 157, so lakeShape is not involved.
findings.fix: Add a guard so the NAIP water class only lowers coastal ground, for example `if (m < 0.5 && h < 20) h = Math.min(h, -2.6 - ...)`. Any threshold between 8.5 and 87 m separates today's real water from the false strip. Add a regression gate, for example in tools/env/test_c3.mjs: over the NAIP coverage, the drop caused by the NAIP override (height with the override vs without it) must be at most 12 m. The drop is 105.6 m today.

findings.problem: The shoreline data marks a strip of the US-101 freeway at the west edge of the coverage as Bay water, and this is the data error behind the pit. The asphalt passes the water rule, and binary_fill_holes cannot restore a non-land region that touches the array border. The shipped land ring (data/sfo_shore.js rings[0], vertices 2-56) therefore has a notch at x -2599..-2499, z -2149..-1939, and the note field declares that notch Bay water.
findings.evidence:
NAIP 2024 crop at world x -2750..-2350, z -2300..-1850 (scratchpad/pit/naip_slot.png) shows the US-101 / I-380 interchange. With the script's own rule on 10 m box-filtered bands, the notch's asphalt has mean NDWI 0.27 and NIR 82, and 78 % of its pixels pass. This contradicts the docstring at line 13 (asphalt 0.07-0.20, NIR >= 114) and the comment at line 57 (dark asphalt NDWI <= 0.20). Adjacent land reads NDWI 0.04.

A replica of lines 49-74 (scratchpad/pit/shore_replica.py, writes nothing to the repo) leaves one non-land component of 2083 px (8332 m²). It touches the west edge only, not the north, east or south edges. Padding the west column as land before fill_holes removes all 2083 px and changes no other pixel (changed bbox: x -2599..-2499, z -2149..-1939). The other water regions that touch the border are real water: NDWI 0.50-0.72, NIR 20-50.
findings.fix: Fill holes with the mainland (west) border treated as land: `land = ndi.binary_fill_holes(np.pad(land, ((0, 0), (1, 0)), constant_values=True))[:, 1:]`. Then regenerate data/sfo_shore.json/.js (the NAIP cache is present in refs/cache/naip) and rebuild the phone artifact (out/phone_artifact/pub) that the films are recorded from. Also correct the asphalt NDWI/NIR claims at lines 13 and 57. Optionally, keep only water components that connect to the regional Bay, so that inland freeway asphalt cannot become 'Bay water' even when it is not enclosed by land.
